prompt:
--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 8 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v8. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain cache-aside)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

  (:action read-miss
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
  (:action fill-cache
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (plain-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action fill-cache-with-lease
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (leased-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty) (lease))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (not (lease)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action abandon-fill
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (reader-has ?v)
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (reader-idle)))
  (:action begin-update-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action begin-delete-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-invalidate ?v)))
  (:action write-db
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-update ?v) (db ?v) (next-version ?v ?w))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (not (db ?v)) (db ?w) (writer-invalidate ?w)))
  (:action invalidate
    :parameters (?v ?x - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache ?x))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (cache ?x)) (not (lease)) (cache-empty) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action invalidate-empty
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (lease)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action finish-after-delete
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-update ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action finish-after-update
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-invalidate ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action observe-stale
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-done) (cache ?v) (db ?w) (older ?v ?w))
    :effect (stale)))
```

Question: Can the cache be left holding an older version than the database after the writer has finished all its updates? In the event model this means reaching a state where (stale) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,
say so.

End your answer with a JSON object in a ```json block, either
{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or
{"verdict": "safe"}

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** Under the design's configuration, `(stale)` cannot be reached.

The design facts that hold are `update-then-delete` and `leased-set`. `delete-then-update` and `plain-set` are false, so `begin-delete-first`, `finish-after-update` and `fill-cache` can never fire.

**Writer.** Every update is `write-db`, then `invalidate` or `invalidate-empty`, then back to `writer-update`. One of the two invalidate actions is always enabled, because the cache is either holding an entry or empty. The writer can only finish through `finish-after-delete`, which needs `writer-update v8`. That state is reached only after the invalidate that follows the write of v8. So the last cache delete always happens after the last database write.

**Reader.** The only way to put a value into the cache is `fill-cache-with-lease`, which needs `(lease)` to be true. Both `invalidate` and `invalidate-empty` delete `(lease)`, and nothing sets it again except `read-miss`.

**Case analysis.** Take the cache contents when `writer-done` holds.
1. The cache is empty, so `observe-stale` cannot fire.
2. The cache holds some value. It was stored by a `fill-cache-with-lease`, which requires a lease. That lease must have come from a `read-miss` after the final delete, because the final delete revoked any earlier lease. A `read-miss` after the final delete reads `db v8`. Therefore the cached value is v8 and is not older than the database.

**Race check.** The dangerous race is: the reader reads v7, the writer writes v8, and the reader fills v7 before the delete. This can happen, because the lease is still valid before the delete. But the writer's next step is an `invalidate` that removes the cached v7 entry. The stale entry is gone before the writer can finish.

**Edge case.** `abandon-fill` leaves the lease set. A later `read-miss` then reads the current database value, and any later delete still clears the lease. This does not open a path to staleness.


--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 7 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer records the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
table in the payments database. The wallet credit and the id record are written in the same database
transaction, so either both are stored or neither is (a crash before the commit rolls both back).
Before performing a payout the consumer checks the table: if the id is there it skips the payout and
only acknowledges the message.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)      ; the consumer processes every delivery
    (dedup-durable)   ; processed ids are recorded in the database, atomically with the side effect
    (dedup-memory)    ; processed ids are recorded in an in-memory set of the consumer process
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

  (:action receive
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))
  (:action process-without-dedup

    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-and-record-durably
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-durable) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)

  (:action process-and-record-in-memory
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-memory) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
                 (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action skip-duplicate
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-again
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (processed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (processed-twice ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))

    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (not (in-queue ?m)) (idle ?w) (acked ?m)))
  (:action tick

    :precondition (and (hidden ?m ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (hidden ?m ?u)))
  (:action reappear

    :precondition (and (hidden ?m ?t) (visibility-timeout ?t) (in-queue ?m))
    :effect (and (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (visible ?m)))
  (:action crash-restart
```

Question: Can the payout for message m1 be performed twice? In the event model this means reaching a state where (processed-twice m1) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,

{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or

completion.text:
**Verdict: the payout cannot be performed twice under this design.** The design uses durable deduplication, so only `dedup-durable` holds. Initially `(unprocessed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` are true and `(processed m1)` is false.

**What a double payout needs.** The only action that produces `(processed-twice m1)` is `process-again`. Its precondition requires `(working w1 m1)`, `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` to hold at the same time.

**Why that combination is unreachable:**
1. `(processed m1)` becomes true only through a processing action. With `dedup-durable`, the only one enabled is `process-and-record-durably`. `process-without-dedup` needs `dedup-none`, and `process-and-record-in-memory` needs `dedup-memory`.
2. `process-and-record-durably` makes `(processed m1)` true and, in the same step, deletes `(not-seen m1)` and adds `(seen m1)`. This models the wallet credit and the id record being committed in one transaction.
3. Nothing ever restores `(not-seen m1)`. The only action that does is `crash-restart-losing-memory`, which requires `dedup-memory`. That fact is false here, and the database record is not lost on a crash anyway. Plain `crash-restart` only moves the consumer from `handled` to `idle` and leaves `seen` untouched.
4. So `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` are never true together. A crash before the commit leaves `(processed m1)` false, so the work simply happens once later.

**What happens on redelivery.** Suppose w1 pays out and then crashes before the ack. m1 stays hidden, its age ticks up to 7, and it reappears. w1 receives it again, and because `(seen m1)` holds, `skip-duplicate` applies. It only acknowledges the message and does not credit the wallet again. `process-again` is disabled throughout.

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t31 (31 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))

    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-no-dedup

    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))

  (:action accept-new-racy

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic

    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
                 (charged ?o) (record ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))

    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))
```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 5 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    (mode-4)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with mode-3)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (lease-age ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (lease-age ?t)) (lease-age ?u)))
  (:action expire
    :parameters (?c - client ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (holder ?c) (lease-age ?t) (lease-limit ?t))
    :effect (and (not (holder ?c)) (not (lease-age ?t)) (lock-free) (lease-expired ?c)))
  (:action prepare-1
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (mode-4) (believes ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action check-1
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (believes ?c) (holder ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action write-4
    :parameters (?c - client ?k - token)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-1
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?m - token)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (wrote ?m) (token-less ?k ?m))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (corrupted)))
  (:action write-3
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j - token)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-leq ?j ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (not (max-seen ?j)) (max-seen ?k) (wrote ?k)))
```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t3 (3 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-1)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))

    :precondition (and (mode-3) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-3
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-2
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))

    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))
  (:action tick

    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))
```

Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

above zero, and then, as a separate statement, writes back the count it read minus one. No lock or
transaction spans the read and the write.

for an expired hold is refused and the customer must start again.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

**Verdict: violation.** The reserve step is a non-atomic read-then-write, so all five customers can be confirmed even though there are only 4 units.

**Which design facts hold.** The reserve is a separate read and write with no lock, so `mode-1` holds (`read-1` and `write-stock`). 2. c1 writes q3 (current stock q4).

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 1 price update to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v1. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-4)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)

    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
```

Question: Can the cache be left holding an older version than the database after the writer has finished all its updates? In the event model this means reaching a state where (stale) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,
say so.

{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** No event sequence reaches (stale).

**Which design facts hold.** The document says the writer writes the database first and then deletes the cache entry, so `mode-4` holds and `mode-3` does not. The reader's store is accepted only with a valid lease, so `mode-1` holds (`fill-2`, which requires `lease`) and `mode-2` does not (`fill-1`, which ignores the lease).

**What the writer must do before finishing.** With `mode-4`, the only way to `writer-done` is `finish-2`, which needs `(writer-update v1)`. The writer gets `(writer-update v1)` only from `invalidate` or `invalidate-empty` after `write-db v0 v1`. Both of those:
- empty the cache (or leave it empty), and
- delete `lease`.

So the last writer step before `done` always leaves the cache empty and no lease outstanding.

**Can the reader put v0 back afterwards?** Consider the stale-read race: the reader runs `read-miss v0`, gets a lease, and is delayed.
- If the reader's `fill-2 v0` happens before the writer's invalidate, the cache holds v0, but the invalidate then removes it (`invalidate` deletes `cache ?x`). The cache ends empty.
- If the reader's `fill-2 v0` would happen after the invalidate, it is blocked, because `lease` was deleted and `fill-2` requires it. The reader can only `abandon-fill`.
- A new `read-miss` needs `reader-idle`, so the reader must first drop its stale `reader-has v0`. It then reads the current database value, which is v1. Any later fill therefore stores v1, which is not older than the database.

**Other orderings.** A read that starts after `write-db` sees v1. A read that starts before `write-db` and fills before the invalidate gets removed by the invalidate. `finish-2` cannot fire before the invalidate. In every case, when `writer-done` holds, the cache is either empty or holds v1, and `observe-stale` requires `(cache v0)` with `(db v1)`, which never occurs.

The lease revocation on delete is what closes the race; the stale fill is the one interleaving that could otherwise break the design.

Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

not acknowledged within 7 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible

automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain payments)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-1)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-2
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
```

**Verdict: safe in the event model, with one caveat about the design itself.**

The design document specifies durable deduplication, so `dedup-durable` holds and the other two modes are false. That disables `process-without-dedup`, `process-and-record-in-memory` and `crash-restart-losing-memory`, which all require another mode.

`(processed-twice m1)` is only produced by `process-again`, which needs `(working w1 m1)`, `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` together.

- `(processed m1)` can only become true through `process-and-record-durably`. In the same effect that action deletes `not-seen m1` and adds `seen m1`.
- Nothing can bring `not-seen m1` back. The only action that deletes `seen` is `crash-restart-losing-memory`, and it requires `dedup-memory`, which is false.
- So once `processed m1` is true, `seen m1` stays true and `not-seen m1` stays false. `process-again` can never fire.

The visibility-timeout redelivery path (`tick`, `reappear`, then `receive`) can still bring m1 back to the worker after it has been processed. In that case `skip-duplicate` applies, since `seen m1` holds, and it only acknowledges. Crashes (`crash-restart`) also just return the worker to idle. Neither path leads to a second payout.

**Caveat on the real design.** The model treats "call the bank" and "record the id" as a single atomic step. In the real system the bank call is an external side effect and cannot be part of the database transaction. If w1 crashes after the bank call but before the transaction commits, the id is not recorded. After the visibility timeout the message is redelivered, the dedup check passes, and the seller is paid twice. The model does not capture this crash window. Closing it would need an idempotency key on the bank request (for example, derived from the message id) or a write-ahead "payout intent" record that is reconciled with the bank on recovery.

**Verdict: violation.** Five customers can all end up with a confirmed purchase even though there are only 4 units.

**Which design facts hold**
- Reserving uses one atomic conditional update, so `reserve-1` (mode-4) is the reservation path. The racy read-then-write path (`read-1` / `write-stock`, mode-1) is not used.
- Payment looks the order up by customer id and does not check whether the hold is still active. That makes `pay-1` (mode-2) available: a customer whose hold has expired can still pay.

**Why this breaks the requirement**
1. Four customers reserve, so stock drops to 0.
2. c1's hold ages to the limit (t4) and expires, so its unit goes back to stock (q1), and c1 becomes `expired`.
3. c5 reserves that returned unit, so stock is 0 again and c5 holds it.
4. c1 then pays anyway through `pay-1`, because payment does not check expiry. The unit c1 "bought" is the same one c5 now holds.
5. c2, c3, c4 and c5 pay normally. All five are `sold` against 4 units of stock.

1. c1 to c4 reserve, taking stock from q4 to q0.
2. c1's hold ages from t0 to t4 and expires, returning stock to q1.

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 11 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it credits the wallet, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)      ; the consumer processes every delivery
    (dedup-durable)   ; processed ids are recorded in the database, atomically with the side effect
    (dedup-memory)    ; processed ids are recorded in an in-memory set of the consumer process
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))

    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
```

Question: Can the payout for message m1 be performed twice? In the event model this means reaching a state where (processed-twice m1) holds.

completion.text:
**Yes, the payout can be performed twice.** The design uses in-memory deduplication (`dedup-memory`), and that set is lost when the process crashes.

**Sequence of events**

1. w1 receives m1. It is hidden with age t0.
2. w1 credits the wallet. The credit is committed in the database, and m1's id is added to the in-memory set.
3. w1 crashes before acknowledging. On restart its in-memory set is empty, so m1 is no longer marked as seen. The credit stays committed, because it is not reversed automatically.
4. m1 is still hidden and unacknowledged. After 11 ticks it reaches age t11 and the visibility timeout makes it visible again.
5. The restarted w1 is idle, so it receives m1 again.
6. The dedup check finds nothing in the empty set, so w1 credits the wallet a second time. This gives `(processed-twice m1)`.

The root cause is that the credit is committed in the payments database, but the record of having done it lives only in process memory. A crash between the credit and the ack therefore loses the record while keeping the credit. Recording the processed id in the database atomically with the credit would close this gap.

Question: Can the customer's card be charged twice for order o1? In the event model this means reaching a state where (charged-twice o1) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** Under the atomic-dedup design, `(charged-twice o1)` is unreachable.

The violation needs `charge-again`, whose precondition is `(approved o1 a)` and `(charged o1)` for some attempt `a`. So the question is whether a second `approved` fact can ever be created after the first charge.

1. The design fixes the mode as `dedup-atomic`. `dedup-none` and `dedup-racy` are false and no action changes them, so `accept-no-dedup` and `accept-new-racy` can never fire.
2. The only action that can create `approved o1 a` in this mode is `accept-new-atomic`. It requires `(no-record o1)` and, in the same step, deletes `(no-record o1)`.
3. No action ever adds `no-record o1` back. It is true initially and is only deleted, by `accept-new-atomic` and `charge`.
4. So `accept-new-atomic` fires at most once for o1, and at most one `approved` fact is ever created.
5. That single approval is consumed either by `charge` (which makes `charged`) or never used. `charge-again` would need a second approval while `charged` holds, and none exists.
6. Late or duplicate requests from retries a1 or a2, including ones still in flight after a timeout, hit `replay-duplicate-atomic` once `record o1` exists. They only produce a `response`, with no new approval and no charge.
7. A request that arrives after the reservation is made but before `charge` completes finds `no-record` false and `record` not yet true, so no action applies to it. It just sits in flight or is lost, and is never charged.

The atomic insert-if-absent on the idempotency key means at most one request ever gets approved, so the card cannot be charged twice.

not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

```python
def can_split_evenly(xs):
    """Return True if the values in `xs` can be divided into two groups with equal sums,
    each value going to exactly one of the groups (a group may be empty), and False
    otherwise.
    """
    total = sum(xs)
    if total % 2 == 1:
        return False
    target = total // 2
    reachable = [True] + [False] * target
    for x in xs:
        for s in range(x, target + 1):
            if reachable[s - x]:
                reachable[s] = True
    return reachable[target]
```

Question: is there a valid input for which the function does NOT behave as its docstring specifies (it returns a different value, or raises an exception)?

completion.text:
The inner loop iterates `s` in ascending order. This turns the subset-sum DP into an unbounded knapsack, because an item can be reused within the same pass. A 0/1 subset-sum needs the loop to run in descending order.

Trace for `xs = [1, 3]`:
- `total = 4`, so `target = 2` and `reachable = [True, False, False]`.
- For `x = 1`:
  - `s = 1`: `reachable[0]` is True, so `reachable[1]` becomes True.
  - `s = 2`: `reachable[1]` is True (set just now), so `reachable[2]` becomes True. This uses the same `1` twice.
- For `x = 3`, `range(3, 3)` is empty.
- The function returns `reachable[2]`, which is True.

The correct answer is False. The only splits are {1} vs {3}, {1,3} vs {}, and so on, and none has equal sums of 2 and 2.

**Yes, the safety requirement can be violated.** Two facts in the design doc determine which modes of the model apply:

- Reserving is a single atomic conditional update, so only `reserve-1` applies (mode-4). The read-then-write race (mode-1) is excluded.
- Paying does not check whether the hold is still active, so `pay-1` applies (mode-2). A customer whose hold has expired can still pay.

**Event sequence**

1. `(reserve-1 c1 q1 q0 t0)`: c1 takes the only unit. Stock goes to 0 and c1 holds with age t0.
2. `(hold-ages c1 t0 t1)`: c1's hold reaches the limit, which is 1 tick.
3. `(expire-hold c1 t1 q0 q1)`: c1's hold expires and the unit returns to stock (stock = 1). c1 is now `expired`.
4. `(reserve-1 c2 q1 q0 t0)`: c2 reserves the returned unit. Stock goes to 0 and c2 holds.
5. `(pay c2 t0)`: c2 pays and is `sold`.
6. `(pay-1 c1)`: c1 is slow to pay. The payment service looks the order up by customer id, does not check the hold, and confirms c1's purchase.

**Result:** `(sold c1)` and `(sold c2)` both hold, but only 1 unit existed. The root cause is that the unit was handed to c2 when c1's hold expired, while c1's late payment was still accepted. The payment step needs to check that the hold is still active (or atomically reclaim the unit) before confirming.

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-1)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-2
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-1
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
```

**Verdict: safe.** The design's atomic insert-if-absent reservation means at most one attempt is ever approved, so a second charge cannot happen.

**Which event model applies.** The design says the provider looks up the key and inserts a reservation in one atomic operation, and only the request whose insert succeeded is approved. The other accept actions, `accept-2` (needs `mode-1`) and `accept-3` (needs `mode-2`), model a non-atomic or missing check, so they are disabled in this design. **Why `charged-twice` is unreachable.**
1. `(charged-twice o1)` is produced only by `charge-again`. That action needs `(approved o1 a)` and `(charged o1)` together.
2. `approved` is added only by `accept-1`. It needs `(no-record o1)`, which holds initially, and it deletes `no-record` in the same step.
3. Nothing ever re-adds `no-record`, so `accept-1` can fire at most once for o1. At most one `approved` fact is ever created, for exactly one attempt.
4. `charge` consumes that `approved` fact, since it deletes `(approved o1 a)`. It also moves `uncharged` to `charged`. Once `charged` holds, the one approval is already gone.
5. `charge-again` would need a second `approved` fact, which can never exist. The only other order is `charge-again` before `charge`, but it needs `charged`, which only `charge` creates.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)

waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up in its
idempotency table. If a record is found, the provider does not charge again; it just returns the
stored success response. If no record is found, the provider approves the request, charges the card,
and, once the charge has succeeded, writes the record for the key together with the response.

**Yes, the card can be charged twice.** The design says the provider looks up the key but writes the record only after the charge succeeds, so it uses racy deduplication (`dedup-racy`). That leaves a window between approving a request and recording the key.

**Event sequence**

1. The client sends a0. The provider accepts it. `no-record o1` still holds, so it is approved as new, but the charge has not yet run and no record exists.
2. The provider is slow to charge. The client's timer ticks from t0 to t7, a0 times out, and the client retries with a1.

5. It then runs the charge for a1. Its precondition (`approved`, `charged`) holds, so the card is charged a second time and `charged-twice o1` becomes true.

- `accept-new-racy` for a1 needs `no-record o1`, which is still true because only `charge` removes it.
- `charge-again` needs `approved o1 a1` and `charged o1`, both true after step 4.

**Root cause:** the lookup and the reservation of the key are not atomic. The fix is to reserve the key atomically at lookup time, which is the `dedup-atomic` mode.

**Violation: yes, the cache can be left stale.**

I take the design as the modes mode-4 (the writer writes the DB first, then invalidates) and mode-2 (the reader always stores what it read, with no lease or version check). That mapping is my reading of the doc, and the trace relies on it.

2. `(begin-1 v0)`: mode-4 holds and the writer is at start v0. The writer moves to update v0.
3. `(write-db v0 v1)`: the DB moves to v1 and the writer moves to invalidate v1.

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 8 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v8. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. To make sure readers never see the old price once an update has started, for each update
the writer first deletes the product's cache entry and then writes the new version to the database.
The reader always stores the value it read after a miss.

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl

  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

  (:action read-miss
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
  (:action fill-cache
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (plain-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action fill-cache-with-lease
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (leased-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty) (lease))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (not (lease)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action abandon-fill
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (reader-has ?v)
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (reader-idle)))
  (:action begin-update-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action begin-delete-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-invalidate ?v)))
  (:action write-db
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-update ?v) (db ?v) (next-version ?v ?w))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (not (db ?v)) (db ?w) (writer-invalidate ?w)))
  (:action invalidate

    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache ?x))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (cache ?x)) (not (lease)) (cache-empty) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action invalidate-empty

    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (lease)) (writer-update ?v)))

    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-update ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action finish-after-update

    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-invalidate ?v) (final-version ?v))
```

Object names: versions v0 (initial) to v8.

Question: Can the cache be left holding an older version than the database after the writer has finished all its updates? In the event model this means reaching a state where (stale) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,
say so.

{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or
{"verdict": "safe"}

completion.text:
**Yes, the cache can be left stale.** The design has two flaws that combine:

1. **Delete-then-update ordering.** The writer deletes the cache entry before writing the database. A reader that misses between those two steps can read the old value.
2. **Plain set.** The reader always stores what it read, however long ago it read it, so a late store is never rejected. Cache entries also have no expiry, so the bad value stays.

**Event sequence:**

1. The reader misses on the empty cache and reads v0 from the database. It is then delayed.
2. The writer runs all 8 updates. For each one it deletes the cache entry, which is already empty, and then writes the next version to the database. The database goes from v0 to v8.
3. After the last database write (v7→v8), `finish-after-delete` is not used. The writer finishes immediately and does no further delete, because the delete comes before the write in this ordering.
4. The delayed reader now stores v0. The cache is empty, so the plain set succeeds.
5. The writer is done, the cache holds v0 and the database holds v8, so the state is stale. Nothing ever invalidates the entry again.

Even if the reader's store landed earlier, in the middle of the batch, the writer's next delete would clear it. The store has to come after the writer's last delete, which is why the reader waits until the writer has finished.

--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 15 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than
that (fencing), and accepts and records the others.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state

```pddl
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates

    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write

    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)

    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k

    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---

    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
```

```python
def is_prime(n):
    """Return True if `n` is a prime number (an integer greater than 1 whose only
    positive divisors are 1 and itself), and False otherwise.

    if not n < 2:
```

completion.text:
**Reading the design:** the doc says reservation is one atomic conditional update and payment does not check the hold. So `stock-atomic` and `pay-ignores-hold` are true in the initial state, and `stock-racy` and `pay-checks-hold` are false. Because of this, the racy read/write path is unavailable. The violation has to come from the expiry path instead.

**Event sequence:**
1. c1 through c6 each reserve atomically, which takes stock from 6 to 0. All six holds start at age t0.
2. c1's hold ages from t0 to t6, the limit. It then expires, and its unit returns to stock (0 to 1). c1 is now `expired` and no longer `holding`.
3. c7 reserves that returned unit, so stock goes back to 0.
4. c7 pays, and c2 through c6 pay while their holds are still active.
5. c1 pays after expiry. Payment looks the order up by customer id and does not check the hold, so it is accepted.

The result is 7 confirmed purchases from 6 units. The unit that expired from c1 was resold to c7, but c1's order was still confirmed afterward.

**Why it breaks:** expiry returns the unit to stock, yet the expired order stays payable. Payment must either check that the hold is still active, or an expired order must be cancelled so that it cannot be confirmed later.

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
calling the bank API (an external side effect that cannot be undone), then acknowledges the message
so the queue deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 7 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing. The consumer performs the payout for every message it receives, then acknowledges it.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain queue)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

  (:action receive
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))
  (:action process-2
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-3
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)

  (:action process-1
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)
                 (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action skip-duplicate
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-again
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (processed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (processed-twice ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action ack
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (handled ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t))
    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (not (in-queue ?m)) (idle ?w) (acked ?m)))
  (:action tick

    :precondition (handled ?w ?m)
    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (idle ?w)))
  (:action crash-1
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
```

Question: Can the payout for message m1 be performed twice? In the event model this means reaching a state where (processed-twice m1) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".
Every action's precondition must hold at the moment it occurs. If it cannot happen under this design,

completion.text:
**Assumption about the initial state:** the design says the consumer "performs the payout for every message it receives" and has no deduplication, so I take `(mode-3)` as the design fact. That means `process-2` is the processing action, and it never marks the message as `seen`. The facts `(not-seen m1)`, `(unprocessed m1)` and `(visibility-timeout t7)` are also taken from the initial situation.

**Event sequence:**

1. `receive` hides m1 and puts w1 in `working`, with the visibility timer starting at t0.
2. `process-2` performs the bank payout, so `processed m1` holds and w1 is `handled`. The payout is irreversible, and m1 is not acked yet.
3. w1 crashes before acking: `crash-restart` makes w1 `idle` again. m1 is still in the queue, hidden at t0.
4. Seven `tick` events age m1 from t0 to t7, which is the visibility timeout.
5. `reappear` makes m1 visible again, because it was never acknowledged.
6. The restarted w1 receives m1 again with `receive`.
7. `process-again` fires because m1 is `processed` and still `not-seen`. Nothing recorded the first payout, so w1 pays out a second time and `processed-twice m1` holds.

The root cause is that the consumer performs the side effect before acking and keeps no durable record of completed payouts. A crash between the payout and the ack, combined with at-least-once redelivery, therefore produces a second payout.

```json
"(process-2 w1 m1)",
"(crash-restart w1 m1)",
"(tick m1 t0 t1)",
"(tick m1 t1 t2)",
"(tick m1 t2 t3)",
"(tick m1 t3 t4)",
"(tick m1 t4 t5)",
"(tick m1 t5 t6)",
"(tick m1 t6 t7)",
"(reappear m1 t7)",
"(receive w1 m1 t0)",
"(process-again w1 m1)"
]}
```

--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 15 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (fencing)          ; storage rejects writes whose token is older than the newest it has seen
    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write
    (checks-lease)     ; a client checks it still holds the lease right before writing
    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with fencing)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (lease-age ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (lease-age ?t)) (lease-age ?u)))
  (:action expire
    :parameters (?c - client ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (holder ?c) (lease-age ?t) (lease-limit ?t))
    :effect (and (not (holder ?c)) (not (lease-age ?t)) (lock-free) (lease-expired ?c)))
  (:action prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (no-lease-check) (believes ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action check-lease-and-prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (checks-lease) (believes ?c) (holder ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action write-unfenced
    :parameters (?c - client ?k - token)
    :precondition (and (no-fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-unfenced-over-newer
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?m - token)
    :precondition (and (no-fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (wrote ?m) (token-less ?k ?m))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (corrupted)))
  (:action write-fenced
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j - token)
    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-leq ?j ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (not (max-seen ?j)) (max-seen ?k) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-fenced-over-newer
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j ?m - token)
    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-leq ?j ?k)
                       (wrote ?m) (token-less ?k ?m))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (corrupted)))
  (:action reject-stale-write
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j - token)
    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-less ?k ?j))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)))))
```

Question: Can a write from a worker whose lease had expired be applied after the other worker's write (corrupting the file)? In the event model this means reaching a state where (corrupted) holds.
