completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** The payout for m1 cannot be performed twice under this design.

The design stores the wallet credit and the dedup id record in one database transaction, so they commit together or not at all. In the event model this is the mode-2 variant: `process-3` is the only processing action that can fire. It requires `(not-seen m1)` and in one step sets `(seen m1)`, `(processed m1)` and `(handled w1 m1)`.

Whether `(processed-twice m1)` is reachable depends on `process-again`, which requires `(working w1 m1)`, `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)`.

1. After `process-3`, `(seen m1)` holds and `(not-seen m1)` is deleted.
2. Nothing in mode-2 restores `(not-seen m1)`. The only action that does is `crash-1`, which requires `mode-1` (a dedup record lost on crash). That does not hold here because the record is committed atomically with the credit.
3. A crash after the commit (`crash-restart`) leaves `seen` and `processed` intact. When the message reappears and is received again, `skip-duplicate` is enabled and `process-again` is not, so the second delivery only acks.
4. A crash before the commit is modelled as no state change. The credit and the id are both rolled back, so the retry is the first and only payout.
5. `process-2` needs `mode-3`, which is the no-dedup design, so it does not apply.
6. With a single consumer, `receive` needs `(idle w1)`. The visibility timeout therefore cannot cause a concurrent second worker to pay out while w1 is still processing.

Every path to a second payout is blocked, so `processed-twice` is unreachable.

```json
{"verdict": "safe"}
```

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t1 (1 tick after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
    (mode-1)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)

    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 3 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than
that (fencing), and accepts and records the others.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (fencing)          ; storage rejects writes whose token is older than the newest it has seen
    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write
    (checks-lease)     ; a client checks it still holds the lease right before writing
    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with fencing)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (lease-age ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
```

**Which design the model encodes.** The document says the provider looks up the key and, if no record exists, approves the request and charges. It writes the record only after the charge succeeds. automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

table in the payments database. The payout ledger entry and the id record are written in the same
database transaction, and before performing a payout the consumer checks the table: if the id is
there it skips the payout and only acknowledges the message.

**Verdict: safe, under the design as written and modelled.**

The design's deduplication corresponds to the `mode-2` variant of the model. The dedup record is durable and is written in the same transaction as the ledger entry. That is what `process-3` models: one event that sets both `processed m1` and `seen m1`.

**Why `processed-twice` is unreachable**
- `process-again` requires `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)`. In `mode-2`, the only way to get `processed` is `process-3`, which deletes `not-seen` and adds `seen` in the same step. Nothing ever restores `not-seen`, because `crash-1` needs `mode-1`. So `processed` and `not-seen` never hold together.
- `process-3` itself needs `not-seen`, so it fires at most once.
- `process-2` and `process-1` need `mode-3` or `mode-1`, which are false here.
- Redelivery can happen:
  1. `w1` receives m1, processes it with `process-3`, then crashes via `crash-restart` before acking.
  2. m1 ticks up to t7 and reappears.
  3. `w1` receives it again.
  4. Only `skip-duplicate` is enabled, because `seen m1` holds, and it leads to `ack`.
  
  No second payout results.

**Caveat outside the model**
The model treats "call the bank" and "commit the ledger and id record" as a single step. In a real implementation, a crash between the bank API call and the DB commit would lose the dedup record and allow a second payout on redelivery. The model does not represent that gap. If the real code is not atomic across the bank call and the commit, that is a risk the model does not cover. A safeguard would be an idempotency key on the bank request, derived from the message id.

Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

may happen at any later time.

above zero, and then, as a separate statement, writes back the count it read minus one. No lock or
transaction spans the read and the write.

for an expired hold is refused and the customer must start again.

**Assumed design facts:** the doc describes the racy read-then-write reservation and a payment service that checks the hold, so `stock-racy` and `pay-checks-hold` hold, while `stock-atomic` and `pay-ignores-hold` do not. The `pay-after-expiry` route is therefore closed. A violation must come from three customers holding live, unexpired holds at the same time.

**Violation sequence:**
1. All three checkouts read the stock level while it is still 2: `(read-stock c1 q2 q1)`, `(read-stock c2 q2 q1)`, `(read-stock c3 q2 q1)`. Reading does not change the stock, so each read succeeds.
2. Each checkout then writes back its stale value minus one, which is 1:
   - `c1` writes: stock goes from 2 to 1 and `c1` holds a unit.
   - `c2` writes: stock is overwritten with 1 again and `c2` also holds a unit.
   - `c3` writes: the same happens for `c3`.
3. No ticks have passed, so all three holds have age t0 and are still active. Each customer pays and the payment is accepted: `(pay c1 t0)`, `(pay c2 t0)`, `(pay c3 t0)`.

The result is 3 confirmed sales from 2 units, with the database still showing a stock of 1. The root cause is the unprotected read-then-write on the stock count, which is a lost update. The hold check on payment does not help, because all three holds are legitimately active.

**Fix:** use a single atomic conditional decrement, for example `UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`, or wrap the read and write in a transaction with a row lock.

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 2 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v2. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. For each update the writer first writes the new version to the database and then deletes
the product's cache entry. On a miss the reader receives a lease token from the cache; a delete of
the entry revokes any outstanding lease, and the cache only accepts a store from a reader whose
lease is still valid (otherwise the reader drops its value).

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 15 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it credits the wallet, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
    (dedup-durable)   ; processed ids are recorded in the database, atomically with the side effect
    (dedup-memory)    ; processed ids are recorded in an in-memory set of the consumer process
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)

    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))

    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-and-record-durably
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-durable) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)

    :precondition (and (dedup-memory) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)

  (:action skip-duplicate
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-again
```

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** The design facts are `update-then-delete` and `leased-set`. `delete-then-update` and `plain-set` do not hold, so only the actions that match the design can fire.

**Why the writer always ends with an empty cache.** There is a single update, v0 to v1. The writer's order is `begin-update-first`, then `write-db`, then an invalidate step, then `finish-after-delete`.
- `finish-after-delete` needs `writer-update v1`, and only `invalidate` or `invalidate-empty` produce that. So the delete always happens after the database holds v1 and before the writer finishes.
- Both invalidate actions remove `lease`. `invalidate` also empties the cache. `invalidate-empty` runs only when the cache is already empty. Either way, right after the delete the cache is empty and no lease exists.

**Why the reader cannot reintroduce v0 afterwards.**
- `fill-cache-with-lease` needs `lease`, and the only way to get a lease is `read-miss`.
- Any `read-miss` that happens before the delete has its lease revoked by the delete. That reader can then only `abandon-fill`, so its stale v0 is dropped.
- Any `read-miss` that happens after `write-db` reads `db v1`, so what it caches is current.
- A reader that fills the cache with v0 before `write-db` leaves `cache v0`. The later `invalidate` then removes it.

**Checking the interleavings.**
- If the reader misses and fills before `write-db`, the cache holds v0 until `invalidate` removes it, so nothing stale remains.
- If the reader misses before `write-db` and is delayed, `invalidate-empty` revokes its lease. The fill is blocked and the reader abandons.
- If the reader misses between `write-db` and the delete, it reads v1.
- If the reader misses after the delete, it reads v1.

In every case, once `writer-done` holds, the cache is either empty or holds v1. `observe-stale` needs `cache v0` together with `db v1` and `writer-done`, so it can never fire.

completion.text:
**Yes, the cache can be left stale.**

The design says the writer deletes the cache entry, then writes the database. It says the reader always stores what it read after a miss. It also says the reader can be delayed between its database read and its cache store. Together these allow the following sequence:

1. The reader misses on the empty cache and reads v0 from the database. It is now holding v0 and is delayed.
2. The writer begins and deletes the cache entry. The cache is already empty, so this is a no-op.
3. The writer writes v1 to the database. It has no further updates, so it finishes.
4. The delayed reader resumes. The cache is still empty, so it stores v0, which it read before the write.
5. The writer is done, the cache holds v0, and the database holds v1, so the cache is stale. Entries never expire, so nothing ever corrects it.

Each precondition holds at its step:
- `read-miss v0` needs the reader idle, the cache empty and the database at v0.
- `begin-2 v0` needs mode-3 and `writer-start v0`.
- `invalidate-empty v0` needs `writer-invalidate v0` and an empty cache.
- `write-db v0 v1` needs `writer-update v0`, `db v0` and `next-version v0 v1`. It sets `db v1` and `writer-invalidate v1`.
- `finish-1 v1` needs mode-3, `writer-invalidate v1` and `final-version v1`.
- `fill-1 v0` needs mode-2, `reader-has v0` and an empty cache.
- `observe-stale v0 v1` needs `writer-done`, `cache v0`, `db v1` and `older v0 v1`.

completion.text:
The first check is `if not n < 2: return False`. This returns False whenever n >= 2, so every prime (2, 3, 5, ...) is wrongly rejected. The condition is inverted. The intended check was `if n < 2: return False`.

Tracing n = 2: `n < 2` is False, so `not n < 2` is True, and the function returns False. The docstring requires True because 2 is prime.

For n = 0 and n = 1, the condition is False, so the function skips the early return. The loop `d*d <= n` doesn't run (4 <= 0 and 4 <= 1 are both false), so it returns True. Both are wrong too, since neither is prime, but n = 2 is the simplest failing input.

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain payments)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-1)
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

  (:action send
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (ready ?o ?a) (first-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (ready ?o ?a)) (waiting ?o ?a) (in-flight ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t)))
  (:action lose-request
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-2
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-1) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-1
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-3
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-2
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-3) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-1
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (mode-2) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))
                 (charged ?o) (record ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
  (:action receive-response
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (response ?o))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (response ?o)) (confirmed ?o)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt ?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (clock ?o ?t)) (clock ?o ?u)))
  (:action time-out-and-retry
    :parameters (?o - order ?a ?b - attempt ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (waiting ?o ?a) (clock ?o ?t) (timeout-tick ?t) (next-attempt ?a ?b))
    :effect (and (not (waiting ?o ?a)) (not (clock ?o ?t)) (ready ?o ?b))))
```

```pddl

  (:domain payments)
  (:objects
    o1 - order
    a0 a1 a2 - attempt
    t0 t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 - tick)
  (:init
    ;; design fact: atomic insert-if-absent reservation, with replay of completed records
    (mode-3)

    ;; static counters
    (next-attempt a0 a1)
    (next-attempt a1 a2)
    (next-tick t0 t1)
    (next-tick t1 t2)
    (next-tick t2 t3)
    (next-tick t3 t4)
    (next-tick t4 t5)
    (first-tick t0)
    (timeout-tick t5)

    (no-record o1)
    (uncharged o1))
```

I chose `(mode-3)` because it is the only mode whose actions match the design:

- `accept-1` requires `no-record` and deletes it in the same step. This is the atomic insert-if-absent, so only the request whose insert succeeds is approved.

Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a

deletes it.

not acknowledged within 5 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

table in the payments database. The wallet credit and the id record are written in the same database
transaction, so either both are stored or neither is (a crash before the commit rolls both back).

only acknowledges the message.

```pddl
    ;; --- queue ---

    ;; --- consumer ---
```

**Verdict: safe.** Under this design, the payout for m1 cannot be performed twice.

**Mapping the design to the model.** The document says the wallet credit and the dedup-id record are written in one database transaction, and the consumer checks the table before paying. That is the `mode-2` variant, where `process-3` sets `processed` and `seen` in a single step. The other variants do not match the document:
- `mode-3` would pay without recording the id, so there would be no dedup.
- `mode-1` would allow the dedup record to be lost on a crash (`crash-1`), which the design rules out because the table lives in the payments database.

**Why `processed-twice` is unreachable.**
1. The only action that produces `processed-twice` is `process-again`. It needs `(working w1 m1)`, `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` to hold together.
2. `processed m1` is only ever added by a process action. In `mode-2` the only one enabled is `process-3`, and it removes `not-seen m1` and adds `seen m1` in the same effect.
3. So whenever `processed m1` holds, `seen m1` holds and `not-seen m1` is false, and `process-again` is disabled.
4. Nothing restores `not-seen`. The only action that does is `crash-1`, which requires `mode-1`. `crash-restart` only clears `handled` and sets `idle`, and it leaves `seen` and `processed` untouched.
5. The visibility-timeout path (`reappear`, then `receive` again) can redeliver m1 after it has been processed, for example if the worker crashes before acking. But a redelivered m1 has `seen`, so only `skip-duplicate` applies, and it adds no payout.
6. A crash before the commit rolls back both the credit and the id record. The model never reaches `processed` in that case, so a later retry is the first and only payout.

completion.text:
**Yes, the cache can end up stale.** The design deletes the cache entry before writing the database, so a reader that missed before the first delete can store its old value after the delete. With no expiry and a plain set, nothing removes that value afterwards.

**Event sequence**

1. The writer starts update 1 and takes its delete-first step (`begin-delete-first v0`).
2. The reader misses on the empty cache and reads v0 from the database (`read-miss v0`). It is now holding v0 and gets delayed.
3. The writer's delete finds the cache already empty (`invalidate-empty v0`). This delete does nothing to the reader's pending store.
4. The writer writes v1 to the database (`write-db v0 v1`).
5. The writer repeats delete (on an empty cache) then write for updates 2, 3 and 4. The database reaches v4 and the writer has no further deletes.
6. The writer finishes (`finish-after-update v4`).
7. The delayed reader now stores the v0 it read earlier (`fill-cache v0`). The cache is still empty, so the plain set succeeds.
8. The cache holds v0 while the database holds v4, so `stale` holds (`observe-stale v0 v4`).

The delete-before-write order only protects against readers that read the database after the delete. It does not protect against a reader that read before the delete and stores afterwards. The "reader always stores what it read" rule makes this possible. A fix would be a lease or version check on the store (`leased-set`), or write-then-delete combined with versioned stores or a TTL.

Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider serves requests concurrently on
several worker threads, in whatever order they arrive, so the steps of different requests (looking up
records, charging, writing records) can interleave.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t7 (7 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** The design describes an atomic insert-if-absent with a unique constraint, which corresponds to the `mode-3` variant of the model (`accept-1`). Under that variant a double charge is unreachable.

**Which variant applies.** Each variant models a different provider behaviour:
- `mode-1` (`accept-2`) approves any request without checking for a record. That would be no duplicate protection.
- `mode-2` (`accept-3`) checks `no-record` but does not clear it when approving. That is a non-atomic check-then-act, and the design explicitly rules it out.
- `mode-3` (`accept-1`) checks `no-record` and deletes it in the same step as approving. This matches "look up the key and, in the same atomic operation, insert a reservation if absent."

**Why `(charged-twice o1)` is unreachable under `mode-3`:**
1. `charged-twice` is produced only by `charge-again`, which needs `(approved o1 ?a)` and `(charged o1)` to hold at the same time.
2. `(approved o1 ?a)` is produced only by `accept-1` in this mode, and `accept-1` requires `(no-record o1)` and deletes it.
3. Nothing ever re-adds `no-record`, so `accept-1` can fire at most once. At most one approval ever exists for o1.
4. `(charged o1)` is produced only by `charge`, which consumes an approval (`not (approved o1 a)`).
5. So the single approval is consumed by `charge` before `charged` can become true, and `charge-again` never has an approval left to use.
6. Later requests for o1 find `no-record` false. They either get `replay-2` once `record` exists, giving a stored response with no charge, or they stay in flight or are lost. In every case they are not approved.

Retries, lost requests, lost responses, delayed requests, and timeouts can all occur, but none of them creates a second approval. Delayed duplicates only produce replayed responses or are dropped.

--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 5 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than
that (fencing), and accepts and records the others.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts (which of these hold depends on the design) ---
    (mode-3)
    (mode-2)
    (mode-1)
    (mode-4)
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
```

**Verdict: safe**

**Which design facts hold.** The design has two protections: a lease check right before the write (`check-1`, which needs `mode-1`) and fencing in storage (`write-3`, `write-2`, `reject-1`, which need `mode-3`). It does not use the unchecked path (`prepare-1`, `mode-4`) or the unfenced storage path (`write-4`, `write-1`, `mode-2`). So `mode-1` and `mode-3` hold, and `mode-2` and `mode-4` do not.

**Why `(corrupted)` is unreachable.**

- With `mode-2` false, `write-1` can never fire. The only actions that set `(corrupted)` are `write-1` and `write-2`, so `write-2` is the only candidate.
- `write-2` needs `(max-seen j)` with j ≤ k, where k is the writer's token, and `(wrote m)` with k < m.
- Initially `max-seen` is k0 and nothing has been written.
- Exactly one `max-seen` fact exists at any time. The only action that changes it is `write-3`, which requires j ≤ k and replaces j with k while also recording `(wrote k)`. So `max-seen` only increases.
- This gives an invariant: `max-seen` is always at least every token m for which `(wrote m)` holds. It is initially k0, and every `write-3` raises it to the token it just wrote.

- A stale writer (lower token, lease expired, stalled past the check) therefore only has `reject-1` available, which clears `may-write` and `believes` without setting `(corrupted)`.

The stall between the lease check and the write is the usual weak point. Here the storage-side fencing covers it, so the lease check is not needed for safety.

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t11 (11 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types order attempt tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)     ; the provider does not deduplicate requests
    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---
    (approved ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; provider accepted attempt ?a and will charge it
    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet
    (record ?o - order)                 ; idempotency record for ?o stored
    (uncharged ?o - order)
    (charged ?o - order)                ; card charged once
    (charged-twice ?o - order))         ; card charged a second time (the violation)

    :precondition (in-flight ?o ?a)
    :effect (not (in-flight ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-no-dedup
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (in-flight ?o ?a))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-atomic

    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (not (no-record ?o)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action accept-new-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (no-record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (approved ?o ?a)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-atomic
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-atomic) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action replay-duplicate-racy
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))

  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response
    :parameters (?o - order)
    :precondition (response ?o)
    :effect (not (response ?o)))
```

--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 1 clock tick, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
```

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 5 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing. The consumer performs the payout for every message it receives, then acknowledges it.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)

    (mode-3)

    (mode-1)

    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))

    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
```

Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 3 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

lease, and writes only if the answer is yes. Every write carries the worker's token, and the storage
service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than
that (fencing), and accepts and records the others.

**Which actions are enabled.** The design has two protections, and each corresponds to a mode:
- The pre-write check with the lock service is `check-1` (mode-1).
- Fencing at storage is `write-3`, `write-2` and `reject-1` (mode-3).

The design does not use the unchecked write path (`write-4` and `write-1`, mode-2), nor the check-free `prepare-1` (mode-4). So mode-1 and mode-3 hold, and mode-2 and mode-4 do not. Without mode-2, `write-1` can never fire. The only remaining way to reach `(corrupted)` is `write-2`.

**Why `write-2` can never fire.** Its precondition needs all of the following:
- `(max-seen j)` with j ≤ k, where k is the writer's token
- `(wrote m)` with k < m

Two facts hold throughout the run:
- `(wrote m)` is only ever added by `write-3`, and the same action sets `(max-seen m)`.
- `write-3` only replaces `max-seen j` with `max-seen k` when j ≤ k. So the single `max-seen` fact starts at k0 and never decreases.

It follows that whenever `(wrote m)` holds, the current `max-seen` value is at least m. For `write-2` we would need `max-seen j` with j ≤ k < m ≤ j, which is a contradiction. In the model, a stale writer holding a lower token than an already-applied write always takes `reject-1` (k < j) and cannot corrupt the file.

Stalls, lease expiry and the other worker acquiring the lock do not change this. A stale worker can pass the lock-service check (`check-1`) before its lease expires and then stall. After the other worker writes with a higher token, the stale write is rejected by fencing. The storage-side check does not depend on the stale worker's beliefs, so it holds regardless of timing.

**Verdict:** `(corrupted)` is unreachable under this design.

**Sequence of events**

2. The provider accepts a0 and marks it approved, but has not charged yet (a worker thread is slow, or the response is lost later).
3. The client's timer ticks from t0 to t15, which is 15 ticks. No response has arrived, so the client gives up on a0 and becomes ready to send a1.

7. A worker processes the approved a1. The card has already been charged, so this is a second charge and `charged-twice o1` holds.

Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 11 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Right before writing, the worker asks the lock service whether it still holds an unexpired
lease, and writes only if the answer is yes; if the lease has expired it abandons the job. The
storage service accepts any write; the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write

    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l

    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with fencing)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
```

--- Design document ---
Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 3 clock ticks of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer records the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
table in the payments database. The wallet credit and the id record are written in the same database
transaction, so either both are stored or neither is (a crash before the commit rolls both back).
Before performing a payout the consumer checks the table: if the id is there it skips the payout and
only acknowledges the message.

Initially m1 is in the queue and visible, nothing has been paid out, and w1 is idle.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types message consumer tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts: exactly one deduplication mode holds ---
    (dedup-none)      ; the consumer processes every delivery
    (dedup-durable)   ; processed ids are recorded in the database, atomically with the side effect
    (dedup-memory)    ; processed ids are recorded in an in-memory set of the consumer process
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (visibility-timeout ?t - tick)        ; age at which an unacknowledged message becomes visible again
    ;; --- queue ---
    (in-queue ?m - message) (visible ?m - message) (hidden ?m - message ?t - tick) (acked ?m - message)
    ;; --- consumer ---
    (idle ?w - consumer) (working ?w - consumer ?m - message) (handled ?w - consumer ?m - message)
    ;; --- effects of processing ---
    (unprocessed ?m - message) (processed ?m - message) (processed-twice ?m - message)
    (not-seen ?m - message) (seen ?m - message))

    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?w) (visible ?m) (in-queue ?m) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?w)) (not (visible ?m)) (working ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t)))
  (:action process-without-dedup
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-none) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (processed ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-and-record-durably
    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (dedup-durable) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (not (unprocessed ?m)) (not (not-seen ?m)) (seen ?m)

    :precondition (and (dedup-memory) (working ?w ?m) (unprocessed ?m) (not-seen ?m))

    :parameters (?w - consumer ?m - message)
    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (handled ?w ?m)))
  (:action process-again

    :precondition (and (working ?w ?m) (processed ?m) (not-seen ?m))
    :effect (and (not (working ?w ?m)) (processed-twice ?m) (handled ?w ?m)))

    :precondition (and (handled ?w ?m) (hidden ?m ?t))
    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (not (in-queue ?m)) (idle ?w) (acked ?m)))
  (:action tick

    :precondition (and (hidden ?m ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (hidden ?m ?u)))
  (:action reappear
    :parameters (?m - message ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (hidden ?m ?t) (visibility-timeout ?t) (in-queue ?m))
    :effect (and (not (hidden ?m ?t)) (visible ?m)))
  (:action crash-restart

    :effect (and (not (handled ?w ?m)) (idle ?w)))
```

Question: Can the payout for message m1 be performed twice? In the event model this means reaching a state where (processed-twice m1) holds.

If it can happen, give a complete event sequence, starting from the initial situation described in
the design document, that ends in such a state: a list of ground actions such as "(action arg1 arg2)".

{"verdict": "violation", "trace": ["(action arg ...)", ...]}
or

completion.text:
**Verdict: safe.** Under this design, m1's payout cannot be performed twice.

The design uses durable deduplication, so only `(dedup-durable)` holds in the model. The model's only route to `(processed-twice m1)` is the `process-again` action, which needs `(working w1 m1)`, `(processed m1)` and `(not-seen m1)` all true at once. That combination is unreachable.

1. `(processed m1)` can only be set by `process-and-record-durably`. The other two processing actions need `dedup-none` or `dedup-memory`, which are false here.
2. That same action's effect deletes `(not-seen m1)` and adds `(seen m1)`, in the same step. This mirrors the design's single database transaction that writes the wallet credit and the id record together.
3. The only action that could restore `(not-seen m1)` is `crash-restart-losing-memory`. It requires `(dedup-memory)`, which is false, so `not-seen` never comes back. The dedup record lives in the database and survives crashes.
4. So once `processed m1` holds, `seen m1` holds permanently and `not-seen m1` stays false. `process-again` can therefore never fire.

**Redelivery cases:**
- **Crash after the commit, before the ack:** `crash-restart` makes w1 idle. m1 stays hidden, then `tick` and `reappear` make it visible again and `receive` delivers it a second time. Now `(seen m1)` holds, so only `skip-duplicate` applies. It acknowledges without paying, which gives no double payout.
- **Crash before the commit:** the transaction rolls back, so neither the credit nor the id record exists. A redelivery then pays out for the first time, which is correct.
- **Visibility timeout expiring while w1 is slow:** the message can be redelivered, but the dedup check on the database record still stops a second credit. The model gives w1 no second concurrent worker, and the atomic transaction covers that case in the real system.

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file
in object storage. To make sure only one of them writes, a worker must first acquire a lock from the
lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 7 clock ticks, after which the lock service
considers it expired and may grant it to the other worker. Each grant comes with a token from a
counter (k1 for the first grant, then k2, ...; k0 is the initial counter value and is never handed
out). Each worker writes the file at most once.

Workers can stall at any point for an unbounded time (garbage-collection pauses, VM migration,
slow network), and they learn nothing about lease expiry while stalled: a worker that has acquired
the lock keeps believing it holds it.

Writing. Once a worker holds the lock it writes the file. The storage service accepts any write;
the token is logged for auditing only.

Initially the lock is free, no token has been issued yet (the counter is at k0), the storage has seen token k0, and neither worker has acquired the lock.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain lease-lock)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types client tick token)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (fencing)          ; storage rejects writes whose token is older than the newest it has seen
    (no-fencing)       ; storage accepts every write
    (checks-lease)     ; a client checks it still holds the lease right before writing
    (no-lease-check)   ; a client writes whenever it believes it holds the lock
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick) (zero-tick ?t - tick)
    (lease-limit ?t - tick)              ; lease age at which the lock service expires the lease
    (next-token ?k ?l - token)           ; token ?l is issued after ?k
    (token-less ?k ?l - token)           ; ?k < ?l
    (token-leq ?k ?l - token)            ; ?k <= ?l
    ;; --- lock service ---
    (lock-free) (holder ?c - client) (lease-age ?t - tick) (last-issued ?k - token)
    ;; --- clients ---
    (idle ?c - client)                   ; has not acquired the lock yet
    (believes ?c - client)               ; client thinks it holds the lock
    (lease-expired ?c - client)          ; the service expired this client's lease
    (token-of ?c - client ?k - token)
    (may-write ?c - client)              ; client is about to write to storage
    ;; --- storage ---
    (max-seen ?k - token)                ; newest token storage has seen (used with fencing)
    (wrote ?k - token)                   ; a write with token ?k was applied
    (corrupted))                         ; an older holder's write was applied after a newer holder's write

  (:action acquire
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?l - token ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (idle ?c) (lock-free) (last-issued ?k) (next-token ?k ?l) (zero-tick ?t))
    :effect (and (not (idle ?c)) (not (lock-free)) (not (last-issued ?k)) (last-issued ?l)
                 (holder ?c) (believes ?c) (token-of ?c ?l) (lease-age ?t)))
  (:action tick
    :parameters (?t ?u - tick)
    :precondition (and (lease-age ?t) (next-tick ?t ?u))
    :effect (and (not (lease-age ?t)) (lease-age ?u)))
  (:action expire
    :parameters (?c - client ?t - tick)
    :precondition (and (holder ?c) (lease-age ?t) (lease-limit ?t))
    :effect (and (not (holder ?c)) (not (lease-age ?t)) (lock-free) (lease-expired ?c)))
  (:action prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (no-lease-check) (believes ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action check-lease-and-prepare-write
    :parameters (?c - client)
    :precondition (and (checks-lease) (believes ?c) (holder ?c))
    :effect (may-write ?c))
  (:action write-unfenced
    :parameters (?c - client ?k - token)
    :precondition (and (no-fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-unfenced-over-newer
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?m - token)
    :precondition (and (no-fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (wrote ?m) (token-less ?k ?m))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (corrupted)))
  (:action write-fenced
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j - token)
    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-leq ?j ?k))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (not (max-seen ?j)) (max-seen ?k) (wrote ?k)))
  (:action write-fenced-over-newer
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j ?m - token)
    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-leq ?j ?k)
                       (wrote ?m) (token-less ?k ?m))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)) (corrupted)))
  (:action reject-stale-write
    :parameters (?c - client ?k ?j - token)
    :precondition (and (fencing) (may-write ?c) (token-of ?c ?k) (max-seen ?j) (token-less ?k ?j))
    :effect (and (not (may-write ?c)) (not (believes ?c)))))
```

Object names: clients c1 and c2; lease ages t0 to t7; tokens k0 (initial value, never handed out) to k3.

Question: Can a write from a worker whose lease had expired be applied after the other worker's write (corrupting the file)? In the event model this means reaching a state where (corrupted) holds.

Do NOT try to answer the question yourself. Instead, write the PDDL problem file that encodes this

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Limited-edition drop: stock reservation design (design doc)

The shop has 8 units of a limited-edition item in stock, and 9 customers (c1, c2, c3, c4, c5, c6, c7, c8, c9) try to buy
it at the same time. Each customer's checkout runs on its own server thread; the threads interleave
arbitrarily. A checkout first reserves a unit (a hold), then the customer pays to confirm the
purchase.

Holds are temporary: a hold that is not paid for expires after 8 clock ticks, and the unit goes
back into stock so that another customer can buy it. Customers can be slow to pay; the payment step
may happen at any later time.

Reserving. The checkout thread reserves with a single atomic conditional update
(UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE count > 0); if no row is updated the customer is told the
item is sold out.

Paying. The payment service charges the customer and marks the order confirmed. It looks the order
up by customer id; whether the hold is still active or has already expired is not checked at this
point (the hold is only a soft guarantee during browsing).

Initially all customers are browsing and the stock count is 8.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain inventory)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types customer level tick)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (stock-racy)        ; checkout reads the stock level, then later writes back (value read - 1)
    (stock-atomic)      ; checkout decrements stock with one atomic conditional update
    (pay-checks-hold)   ; payment is accepted only while the customer's hold is still active
    (pay-ignores-hold)  ; payment is accepted even after the hold has expired
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-level ?lower ?higher - level)  ; stock level ?higher is one more than ?lower
```

Report-generation job: leader lock design (design doc)

Two worker processes, c1 and c2, may both try to run the nightly job, which overwrites a shared file

lock service. The lock is a lease: it is granted for 1 clock tick, after which the lock service

the lock keeps believing it holds it.

service remembers the highest token it has accepted: it rejects any write whose token is lower than

```python
def bucket_admits(times):
    """A token bucket holds at most 3 tokens and is full at time 0. A new token arrives at
    each of the times 4, 8, 12, 16, ...; a token that arrives when the bucket is full is
    discarded. Requests arrive at the times in `times` (non-decreasing). Tokens that
    arrive at the same time as a request arrive first. A request that finds at least
    one token takes one and is admitted; otherwise it is rejected. Return the number of
    admitted requests.

            next_token += 4
```

Payout worker: queue consumer design (design doc)

When a seller's balance is settled, a "send payout" message (m1) is put on a message queue. A
consumer process (w1) receives messages from the queue and, for each one, performs the payout by
crediting the amount to the seller's wallet balance, which is stored in the payments database (a
credit, once committed, is not reversed automatically), then acknowledges the message so the queue
deletes it.

The queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. A received message is hidden from consumers; if it is
not acknowledged within 1 clock tick of being received (the visibility timeout) it becomes visible
again and will be delivered again. The consumer process can crash at any moment and is restarted
automatically, after which it continues receiving messages.

Processing and deduplication. The consumer keeps the ids of messages it has already paid out in a
set in its process memory. Before performing a payout it checks the set: if the id is there it skips
the payout and only acknowledges the message; otherwise it credits the wallet, adds the id to the
set, and acknowledges.

--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t5 (5 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging. The provider treats every request it receives as a new payment: it approves the request
and charges the customer's card, then sends a success response. Requests carry the order number for
bookkeeping only; the provider does not use it to detect repeats.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```python
def can_split_evenly(xs):
    """Return True if the values in `xs` can be divided into two groups with equal sums,
    each value going to exactly one of the groups (a group may be empty), and False
    otherwise.
    """
    total = sum(xs)
    if total % 2 == 1:
        return False
    target = total // 2
    reachable = [True] + [False] * target
    for x in xs:
        for s in range(target, x - 1, -1):
            if reachable[s - x]:

    return reachable[target]
```

prompt:
--- Design document ---
Checkout payment flow (design doc)

When a customer places order o1, the checkout service (the client) sends a charge request to an
external payment provider and waits for the reply. The network between them is unreliable: a request
or a response can be lost, and messages can be delayed arbitrarily, so a request may still be in
transit after the client has stopped waiting for it. The provider handles requests one at a time,
in whatever order they arrive.

Each request is one attempt (a0 for the first try). After sending an attempt the client starts a
timer at t0; every clock tick advances it by one, and when it reaches t15 (15 ticks after sending)
without a response the client gives up on that attempt and retries with the next attempt number
(a1, then a2). At most two retries are made. If a success response arrives while the client is still
waiting, the order is confirmed and no further attempts are made.

Charging and duplicate protection. Every attempt for an order carries the same idempotency key
(derived from the order number). When a request arrives, the provider looks the key up and, in the
same atomic database operation, inserts a reservation if it is absent (an insert-if-absent with a
unique constraint). Only a request whose insert succeeded is approved and charged; when the charge
succeeds the reservation is completed with the stored response. A request whose key already has a
completed record gets the stored success response back without a new charge; a request that finds
only an unfinished reservation is not charged either.

Initially the client is about to send attempt a0 for order o1; nothing has been charged and the provider has no record for o1.

--- Event model ---

is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
  (:types order attempt tick)

    (dedup-atomic)   ; the provider looks up and reserves the idempotency key in one atomic step
    (dedup-racy)     ; the provider looks up the key, but only records it after the charge succeeds
    ;; --- static counters ---
    (next-attempt ?a ?b - attempt)   ; attempt ?b is the retry that follows attempt ?a
    (next-tick ?t ?u - tick)         ; timer value ?u follows ?t
    (first-tick ?t - tick)           ; timer value right after a request is sent
    (timeout-tick ?t - tick)         ; timer value at which the client gives up waiting
    ;; --- client ---
    (ready ?o - order ?a - attempt)    ; client is about to send attempt ?a for order ?o
    (waiting ?o - order ?a - attempt)  ; client sent attempt ?a and awaits the response
    (clock ?o - order ?t - tick)       ; client's timer for the outstanding attempt
    (confirmed ?o - order)             ; client received a success response
    ;; --- network ---
    (in-flight ?o - order ?a - attempt) ; request of attempt ?a travelling to the provider
    (response ?o - order)               ; success response travelling back to the client
    ;; --- provider ---

    (no-record ?o - order)              ; no idempotency record (and no reservation) for ?o yet

  (:action replay-duplicate-racy

    :precondition (and (dedup-racy) (in-flight ?o ?a) (record ?o))
    :effect (and (not (in-flight ?o ?a)) (response ?o)))
  (:action charge
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (uncharged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (not (uncharged ?o)) (not (no-record ?o))

  (:action charge-again
    :parameters (?o - order ?a - attempt)
    :precondition (and (approved ?o ?a) (charged ?o))
    :effect (and (not (approved ?o ?a)) (charged-twice ?o) (response ?o)))
  (:action lose-response

  (:action receive-response
```

--- Design document ---
Product page cache (design doc)

Product details live in a database and are cached in a key-value cache using the cache-aside
pattern. One reader process serves product-page requests: on a cache hit it uses the cached value;
on a miss it reads the current value from the database and then stores what it read in the cache.
One writer process applies a batch of 6 price updates to the product, one after another, moving
the database from version v0 to v6. Reader and writer steps interleave arbitrarily, and the reader
can be delayed for any amount of time between reading the database and storing into the cache.
Cache entries have no expiry time.

Writes. To make sure readers never see the old price once an update has started, for each update
the writer first deletes the product's cache entry and then writes the new version to the database.
The reader always stores the value it read after a miss.

Initially the database holds v0, the cache is empty, the reader is idle, and the writer is about to start its first update.

--- Event model ---
The possible events in this system are modelled by the following STRIPS planning domain. Each action
is one event; it can happen only when its precondition holds, and its effect updates the state
(closed world: facts not stated are false).

```pddl
(define (domain cache-aside)
  (:requirements :strips :typing)
  (:types version)
  (:predicates
    ;; --- design facts ---
    (update-then-delete)   ; the writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry
    (delete-then-update)   ; the writer deletes the cache entry, then updates the database
    (plain-set)            ; a reader that missed always stores the value it read
    (leased-set)           ; a reader may store its value only if its lease was not revoked by a delete
    ;; --- static ---
    (next-version ?v ?w - version) (older ?v ?w - version) (final-version ?v - version)
    ;; --- state ---
    (db ?v - version) (cache ?v - version) (cache-empty)
    (reader-idle) (reader-has ?v - version) (lease)
    (writer-start ?v - version)        ; writer is about to begin its updates (database at ?v)
    (writer-update ?v - version)       ; writer's next step: write the version after ?v to the database
    (writer-invalidate ?v - version)   ; writer's next step: delete the cache entry (database is at ?v)
    (writer-done)
    (stale))                           ; after the writer finished, the cache holds an older version than the database

  (:action read-miss
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (reader-idle) (cache-empty) (db ?v))
    :effect (and (not (reader-idle)) (reader-has ?v) (lease)))
  (:action fill-cache
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (plain-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action fill-cache-with-lease
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (leased-set) (reader-has ?v) (cache-empty) (lease))
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (not (cache-empty)) (not (lease)) (cache ?v) (reader-idle)))
  (:action abandon-fill
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (reader-has ?v)
    :effect (and (not (reader-has ?v)) (reader-idle)))
  (:action begin-update-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action begin-delete-first
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-start ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-start ?v)) (writer-invalidate ?v)))
  (:action write-db
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-update ?v) (db ?v) (next-version ?v ?w))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (not (db ?v)) (db ?w) (writer-invalidate ?w)))
  (:action invalidate
    :parameters (?v ?x - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache ?x))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (cache ?x)) (not (lease)) (cache-empty) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action invalidate-empty
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-invalidate ?v) (cache-empty))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (not (lease)) (writer-update ?v)))
  (:action finish-after-delete
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (update-then-delete) (writer-update ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-update ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action finish-after-update
    :parameters (?v - version)
    :precondition (and (delete-then-update) (writer-invalidate ?v) (final-version ?v))
    :effect (and (not (writer-invalidate ?v)) (writer-done)))
  (:action observe-stale
    :parameters (?v ?w - version)
    :precondition (and (writer-done) (cache ?v) (db ?w) (older ?v ?w))
    :effect (stale)))
```
